title: Can You Wear Red to a Wedding
metaTitle: Can You Wear Red to a Wedding? Etiquette & Culture Guide
metaDescription: Can you wear red to a wedding? Yes at most Western weddings, but not where red is the bride's color. Verdicts for Chinese, Indian, black tie and men.
h1: Can You Wear Red to a Wedding? What Etiquette Experts and Wedding Traditions Say
answer: Yes, at most American and Western weddings. Etiquette expert Elaine Swann calls the no-red rule "another internet fable." Match the red to the formality, with deep reds and burgundy for evening, fall and holiday weddings. The real exception is a Chinese, Indian or Vietnamese wedding, where red is a bridal color: wear something else unless the family says otherwise. Men can wear a red tie or pocket square almost anywhere.
intro: Can you wear red to a wedding? At a typical American wedding, yes: two named etiquette experts quoted in national media say so, with one caveat about how loud the red is. The answer changes completely at a wedding where red is the bride's color, which is the case in Chinese, Indian and Vietnamese traditions. Between those two poles sit the questions people actually search for: is it rude, does burgundy count, can you wear red to a black tie wedding, and what about a red suit or tie for men. Each gets a direct answer below, along with the verdict table.

contentSections.heading: Two etiquette experts, one rule, and a disagreement about how loud
contentSections.content:
The idea that red is off limits for wedding guests has no clear origin in etiquette writing. TODAY's January 2026 report covers the debate as it played out on TikTok, where theories range from red signaling that you are a former partner of the groom to red simply upstaging the bride. Elaine Swann, the etiquette expert TODAY consulted, rejects it: red is "perfectly acceptable" at weddings, the rule is "another internet fable," and "especially here in the U.S., red denotes the color of love." Her closing advice is "Wear what looks great on you."

Swann gave Who What Wear the same verdict earlier, adding that red "is a very festive color and goes quite well, especially for fall and holiday-season weddings."

Diane Gottsman, also quoted by Who What Wear as an etiquette expert, is more cautious: "Red is always a risk if good judgment isn't involved. A bright red [or] loud crowd-stopping red is not appropriate. A muted cranberry, perhaps with a pattern, is probably fine." She adds that when in doubt she would prefer guests not take the risk.

Read together, the two positions are closer than they look. Neither says red itself is rude. They differ on how much attention a guest's outfit should draw. So the safe reading is: red is allowed; a deeper or patterned red is allowed nearly everywhere; a bright red statement gown is the version to save for an evening wedding where everyone is dressed up.

contentSections.heading: Red belongs to the bride in Chinese, Indian and Vietnamese weddings
contentSections.content:
This is the exception that matters, because it turns red from a style choice into a real breach.

Chinese weddings. Wikipedia's article on Chinese marriage says that in modern weddings the bride generally picks red, following Chinese tradition, or white, the more Western choice, and describes red in the traditional procession as symbolizing happiness. The article on color in Chinese culture adds that red is associated with good fortune, wealth and happiness and is frequently used in weddings. Swann told Who What Wear that at Chinese and Indian weddings "it is highly inappropriate to wear the color red," noting that the bride will typically wear two dresses, one of them traditionally red.

Indian weddings. Wikipedia's article on the wedding sari says wedding saris are usually red, a color associated with married women, though color combinations vary by region, caste and religion. Vogue's guide to wedding colors makes the same point: red is a traditional color for brides in China and India.

Vietnamese weddings. Wikipedia's article on the traditional Vietnamese wedding says reds and pinks remain a popular choice for brides, and that brides may also wear a Western white gown for the church or civil ceremony. Other guests wear their own áo dài or formal Western clothes.

What to do: at any of these weddings, choose a color that is neither red nor white. White is the traditional mourning color in Chinese culture, according to both Wikipedia's mourning and Chinese color articles, so it is doubly wrong there. If you are unsure which traditions the couple will follow, ask them or a family member; it is a normal question and an easy one to answer.

contentSections.heading: Match the red to the formality, the season and the hour
contentSections.content:
Where red is allowed, the shade and fabric do the same work they do for any color: they tell people whether you understood the dress code.

Black tie and formal evening weddings are the easiest place to wear red. Emily Post's black tie list for women, a formal floor-length evening gown, a dressy cocktail dress or your dressiest little black dress, sets length and fabric, not color, so a deep red gown in satin, velvet or crepe meets the code. So can you wear red to a wedding with a black tie dress code? Yes, in a gown.

Cocktail and semi-formal weddings suit a red cocktail dress or dressy separates in a jewel-deep shade. If the wedding starts after 6 p.m., Emily Post's semi-formal advice is to err on the side of formality.

Festive and holiday weddings practically invite it. Emily Post's festive code tells women to feature holiday colors and lists a festive or holiday-themed tie for men.

Daytime, garden and beach weddings are where Gottsman's caution applies most. A bright red solid in full sun is the loudest thing in every photograph. A red print, a softer brick or coral, or red as an accent on a dress of another color reads as celebration without the spotlight.

Burgundy, wine and cranberry are reds for etiquette purposes, so they carry the same cultural exception, and cranberry is the shade Gottsman singles out as "probably fine" elsewhere. For a fall or winter wedding they are among the safest saturated colors you can choose.

contentSections.heading: Red for men: ties, pocket squares and the rare red suit
contentSections.content:
Men's red questions are mostly about accents, and accents are easy.

A red tie, bow tie or pocket square is a normal wedding accessory. Emily Post's festive code lists a tie that is festive or holiday-themed, and creative black tie allows a matching colored or patterned bow tie and cummerbund with a tuxedo. At a standard black tie wedding the bow tie should be black, per the same guide.

A burgundy or deep red dinner jacket sits in creative black tie territory: Emily Post describes that code as a tuxedo with trendy or whimsical items. Under plain black tie, stick to the black tuxedo, or the white dinner jacket the guide permits in summer, the tropics or on a cruise.

A full red suit is the men's equivalent of a bright red statement gown. It is permitted at festive or creative codes but draws the same attention, so it is a poor choice at a traditional or daytime wedding.

At a Chinese, Indian or Vietnamese wedding, a small red accent is a different matter from a red outfit, but none of the sources read for this page addresses it directly. If you want to wear a red tie there, ask the couple first.

contentSections.heading: Red is a smaller worry than white or black, in real posts
contentSections.content:
In our analysis of 10,700 posts on r/Weddingattireapproval (16 April – 21 October 2026), 350 posts (3.3%) mention red, excluding the phrase "red flag". Method: we searched every post's title and body for each color word and counted the posts that contain it at least once.

Red ranks well below the colors that worry guests most. White appears in 19.3% of posts (excluding "white tie") and black in 10.6% (excluding "black tie"), while red sits alongside gold and navy. The burgundy family (burgundy, maroon, wine or oxblood) appears in 222 posts, 2.1%.

The flair with the highest share of red mentions is the general Wedding Question flair, at 6.3%, which fits a question about whether a color is allowed rather than whether a particular outfit fits a dress code.

The cultural counts are small but point the same way as the etiquette sources. Of 96 posts mentioning Indian, Hindu, Desi, South Asian, Sikh or Punjabi weddings, 17 also mention red; of 22 posts mentioning Chinese weddings, 3 do.

contentSections.heading: Skip red in four situations, and wear this instead
contentSections.content:
Choose another color when:

• The wedding follows Chinese, Indian or Vietnamese tradition and the family has not told you red is welcome.
• The bridesmaids, the groomsmen's ties or the couple's published palette are red.
• The bride is wearing red, for any reason.
• The wedding is a daytime ceremony and your red is a bright solid that will be the loudest thing in the photographs.

Alternatives that keep the depth and formality of red: emerald, sapphire, plum, deep teal and navy all work in the same fabrics and photograph richly in evening light. At a Chinese wedding, avoid white as well as red. If you love red but the situation calls for caution, wear it as an accent, in a print or a small accessory, rather than head to toe. For dresses in deep reds suitable for evening and fall weddings, see the red wedding guest dresses page.

How to ask without making it awkward. A short message to the couple or a family member does the job: name the wedding, say you are choosing an outfit, and ask whether there are any colors they would rather guests avoid. Couples whose bride will change into a red outfit at some point in the day will usually be glad you checked, and couples who have no preference will tell you so in one line. If you cannot ask, read the wedding website and the invitation again. A traditional ceremony listed alongside the Western one, or a request that guests wear áo dài or other traditional dress, tells you which tradition is in play, and with it whether red is the bride's color.

faqs.question: Why can't you wear red to a wedding?
faqs.answer: At most Western weddings you can. The rule is folklore: Elaine Swann calls it "another internet fable," and TODAY reports the recent debate as a TikTok one. The real reasons to avoid red are a bridal-red tradition (Chinese, Indian, Vietnamese weddings), a red bridal-party palette, or a bright red that would upstage the couple at a daytime wedding.

faqs.question: Can you wear red to a Chinese wedding?
faqs.answer: Avoid it. Red is a traditional bridal color in Chinese weddings, and Swann says it is highly inappropriate for guests there. Avoid white too, which is the traditional Chinese mourning color. Choose a jewel tone such as blue, green or purple unless the family tells you otherwise.

faqs.question: Can you wear red to an Indian wedding?
faqs.answer: Avoid it unless the family says it is welcome. Wikipedia notes that wedding saris are usually red, a color associated with married women, and Swann advises guests not to wear red at Indian weddings. Colors vary by region, caste and religion, so asking the family is the most reliable route.

faqs.question: Is burgundy OK for a wedding guest?
faqs.answer: Yes at most Western weddings, and it is one of the safest saturated colors for fall and winter. Diane Gottsman singles out a muted cranberry as probably fine. Treat burgundy as red for cultural purposes, though: skip it at Chinese, Indian and Vietnamese weddings unless you are told it is welcome.

faqs.question: Can you wear red to a black tie wedding?
faqs.answer: Yes. Emily Post's black tie code sets length and fabric, not color, so a floor-length gown in deep red satin, velvet or crepe meets it. Men should keep to the black tuxedo and black bow tie; a red bow tie belongs to creative black tie.
